vignette:
He is twenty-five now, a European man who sells phone contracts and home internet packages from a bright retail kiosk in a shopping center, but the rhythm of ordinary customer service still competes with another rhythm in his body, one learned in a war zone. He lives with his girlfriend in a small apartment and tries hard to be the version of himself that belongs in this quieter life. From the outside, he can look composed: clean shirt, practiced smile, easy pitch. Over several conversations, though, his story unfolds as a life still organized around danger.

A few years earlier, he is living in a civilian neighborhood where shelling has become part of daily life. At first he tells himself that people adapt to anything. He learns which stairwells feel safer, how to sleep in clothes, how to distinguish distant gunfire from something close enough to matter. He goes out for bread and cigarettes when the street is briefly calm. He calls his mother to say he is fine even when windows have just rattled from blasts nearby. The fear is constant but practical, trimmed down to decisions: run or wait, stay low or cross now, conserve phone battery, find water.

The event he returns to most often happens in daylight. He is moving with other civilians toward what they think will be a safer area. There is a sudden explosion close enough to throw him down. For a few seconds he cannot hear anything but a high, electrical ringing. Dust fills his mouth. When he lifts his head, the street has changed shape. A car is burning. Someone near him is screaming for help, then stops. He sees a man lying in a way that does not look possible. He remembers trying to crawl rather than stand, because standing feels like volunteering to be shot. He does not know where to look first: at the injured, at the sky, at the ground under his hands. The helplessness shames him almost as much as the terror. He still says, “I should have done more,” though at the time he is a young civilian trying simply to stay alive.

After that day, his body no longer waits for evidence before reacting. He startles at any sharp noise. He scans windows, rooftops, exits. Sleep becomes thin and unreliable. If he dozes, he jerks awake sweaty, heart pounding, convinced for a moment that the room is collapsing. He becomes irritable in ways that surprise him. People around him are also frightened, also exhausted, and there is little space to speak about any of it. He feels himself narrowing into survival mode: less future, less language, less trust.

When he finally leaves the war zone, others describe him as lucky. He uses that word too, but it lands strangely. In the safer country where he settles, grocery stores are full, buses run on time, and people complain about small inconveniences with an innocence he cannot share. His girlfriend knows some of what happened, but not always the texture of it. At night, if she shifts suddenly in bed, he can come awake swinging his arm or scrambling to the floor before he realizes where he is. He hates the look on her face when she is frightened of him. On bad nights he stays on the couch so he can watch the window and avoid the shame of startling her awake.

Work in sales gives him structure and a script. He is good at reading people quickly, noticing tone, tracking mood changes before customers say anything directly. In another life these might simply be professional strengths. In his life they are tied to hypervigilance. He positions himself where he can see the entrance. If a child drops a metal water bottle nearby, his stomach flips and his whole body braces before his mind catches up. During holiday promotions, when the mall is crowded and loud, he feels trapped inside his own skin. He smiles through conversations about data plans while sweat gathers under his shirt. Sometimes he escapes to the stockroom, stands very still, and tells himself he is in a mall, not under bombardment. He feels embarrassed that fluorescent lights and a popping balloon can reduce him to this.

He avoids news from home and then compulsively checks it late at night. He does not like driving certain routes because overpasses and roadside debris pull him instantly back into old calculations. He keeps extra bottled water, chargers, canned food, and cash in the apartment, not as a hobby but because not being prepared feels intolerable. His girlfriend calls him tense; he hears accusation even when she means concern. Small disagreements can flare quickly. He becomes cold, withdrawn, and unreachable, then later flooded with guilt. He misses the man he imagines he was before the war—more open, more spontaneous, less suspicious of peace.

What troubles him most is not only the fear but the distance it creates. He can laugh with coworkers, hit his sales targets, cook dinner with his girlfriend, and still feel as if part of him remains on that street, ears ringing, mouth full of dust, waiting for the next blast. He wants ordinary things—a stable job, a future with his partner, sleep that feels like rest—but ordinary life still arrives to him through the filter of catastrophe. Even now, in safety, his body keeps insisting that safety is temporary.
